title: Longitudinal study highlights the enduring toll of childhood loneliness and social isolation d-social-isolation/
author: Eric W. Dolan
summary: Eric Dolan reports on a King's College London study published in Development and Psychopathology that followed 2,232 twins from age 12 to 18. It tests the popular evolutionary idea that loneliness works like hunger, a signal that pushes isolated people to reconnect. The data do not support it: loneliness and social isolation fed into each other over time, and lonely children were more, not less, likely to be isolated at 18. Both independently predicted poorer mental health, well-being and socioeconomic outcomes, and isolation was two to three times as strong a predictor of education and employment problems as childhood depression or anxiety. The most isolated children had about 2.4 times the odds of being not in education, employment or training. The author notes limits including only two measurement points, differing measures and a twin sample, and the researchers suggest tackling loneliness and isolation directly.
points: Loneliness did not motivate isolated children to rebuild relationships, undermining the idea that it acts as a helpful alarm signal.
Childhood loneliness predicted later social isolation about twice as strongly as isolation predicted later loneliness.
Social isolation at 12 predicted fewer qualifications and lower employability, with odds of being NEET at 18 about 2.4 times higher.
Isolation's effect on education and employment was two to three times stronger than for childhood depression or anxiety, a blind spot for skills-focused youth employment strategies.
Limitations include just two time points, different instruments at each age and a twin-only sample.
quotes: The findings challenge the idea that feeling lonely serves as a helpful biological alarm bell that pushes young people to repair their social bonds.
The researchers found that loneliness and social isolation feed into each other over time, rather than correcting one another.
Isolated children who experienced high loneliness went on to experience high levels of social isolation as young adults, just like their peers who were isolated but not lonely.

The risk of becoming NEET (not in education, employment or training) was particularly striking: the most isolated children had around 2.4 times the odds of being NEET at 18, compared with their peers.
What surprised us most was the strength of the association between social isolation and poor education and employment outcomes,” Bryan said.
